en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Refutation of the Puzzles (Meṇḍakapañha) — The Section on What is Set Aside (Paṇāmitavagga)
12. The Question on What is Offered by a Bhikkhu “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘I am one who is free from anger and devoid of harshness. Yet again, the Tathāgata [reproved] the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna together with their retinues.”
"He dismissed them. "Venerable Nāgasena, was the Tathāgata angry when he dismissed the assembly, or was he pleased when he dismissed them?
First, you must explain this: what was his name?

"If, venerable Nāgasena, he dismissed the assembly while angry, then the Tathāgata’s anger was not overcome. If, on the other hand, he dismissed them while pleased, then he dismissed them without cause and without knowing [the situation]."
“This too is a double-edged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘I am free from anger and devoid of harshness. And yet, the elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna were dismissed along with their retinues, and that was not out of anger.”

“In this case, great king, suppose a certain man were to stumble and fall upon the great earth—upon a root, a stump, a rock, a pebble, or on uneven ground. Would the great earth, great king, be angry and cause him to fall?
“Certainly not, venerable sir. The great earth has neither anger nor favor; the great earth is free from both attraction and aversion. That lazy man simply stumbled and fell of his own accord.”

“In the same way, Great King, there is neither anger nor favoritism in the Tathāgatas; the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are entirely free from attachment and aversion. Rather, they have been sent away by their own offense, committed by themselves.
Furthermore, Great King, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse; whatever dead corpse is in the great ocean, it quickly casts it out and washes it onto the shore.
Now, Great King, does the great ocean cast that corpse out because it is angry?”
“Indeed not, venerable sir; the great ocean has neither anger nor favor; the great ocean is free from attachment and aversion.

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgatas have neither anger nor favor; the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are free from attachment and aversion. Rather, they are dismissed because of their own offense committed by themselves.
Just as one who stumbles on the earth falls down, so too one who stumbles in the sublime teaching of the Conqueror is dismissed.”
“Just as, Great King, a dead corpse is cast out from the ocean, so too is one who has stumbled cast out from the sublime teaching of the Conqueror.

But when the Tathāgata casts them out, Great King, it is because he desires their welfare, their benefit, their happiness, and their purification, thinking: ‘In this way they will be completely liberated from birth, aging, sickness, and death’—it was for this reason that he cast them out.”
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This was the twelfth question, concerning what is sent away.
This was the third chapter, on what is sent away.
In this chapter, there are twelve questions.
